facts.text: In the Roman town of Pompeii, dirty water often ran down the streets, so stepping stones were placed across them for people on foot.
When the first Highway Code came out in 1931, more than 7,000 people were being killed on Britain's roads each year.
In 1934, Britain marked new pedestrian crossings with rows of studs in the road and Belisha beacons.
A traditional Belisha beacon is an orange (amber) globe on top of a tall black-and-white pole that warns drivers of a crossing.
The beacons were named after Leslie Hore-Belisha, the minister of transport who introduced them.
By the late 1940s, people were paying less attention to the crossings, and in 1949 the government tested new road markings to make them easier to see.
In 1951, black-and-white stripes with a beacon on each side of the road were approved as the zebra crossing.
